q: Why does scarcity remain even when a society becomes wealthier?
options: Every product becomes physically scarce under the stated conditions.
Wealth eliminates the need to choose in the situation described.
Available resources and time are still limited relative to wants.
Higher income automatically creates shortages for the decision being evaluated.
correctAnswer: Available resources and time are still limited relative to wants.
commonError: Treating scarcity as a problem only for poor societies.
feedback: Scarcity persists because resources and time remain limited relative to competing wants.

q: A free campus workshop still involves scarcity because:
options: No one pays a money price.
Seats, instructor time, and student time are limited.
The topic is not important.
The workshop creates a legal price ceiling.
correctAnswer: Seats, instructor time, and student time are limited.
commonError: Assuming a zero money price means no scarce resources are used.
feedback: A zero price does not eliminate limits on space, labor, or time.

q: A city can fund either a new fire station or several neighborhood parks with the same budget. This illustrates:
options: The elimination of scarcity through taxation.
A tradeoff created by limited public resources.
A shortage caused by a price ceiling.
A gain from specialization.
correctAnswer: A tradeoff created by limited public resources.
commonError: Missing the tradeoff because both projects are socially valuable.
feedback: Limited funds force the city to choose among competing uses.

q: A student has three free hours and wants to study, work, exercise, and sleep more. The central economic problem is:
options: The student must choose the option with the highest money return.
The student faces no scarcity because time has no price.
The student cannot fully satisfy all competing uses of time.
Only the work option has a cost.
correctAnswer: The student cannot fully satisfy all competing uses of time.
commonError: Ignoring time as a scarce resource.
feedback: Time is scarce, so not every desired activity can be expanded at once.

q: Which statement best distinguishes efficiency from equality?
options: Efficiency means everyone receives the same outcome as the relevant economic conclusion.
Efficiency and equality always move together as the relevant economic conclusion.
Efficiency concerns total gains from resources; equality concerns how those gains are distributed.
Equality means producing the maximum possible output as the relevant economic conclusion.
correctAnswer: Efficiency concerns total gains from resources; equality concerns how those gains are distributed.
commonError: Treating efficiency and equality as synonyms.
feedback: Efficiency focuses on the size of the economic pie; equality focuses on its distribution.

q: A new technology doubles crop yields. What happens to scarcity?
options: Scarcity disappears permanently as the relevant economic conclusion.
The technology removes all tradeoffs from production as the relevant economic conclusion.
Scarcity becomes a temporary shortage only as the relevant economic conclusion.
Scarcity is reduced for some goods but not eliminated because wants and other constraints remain.
correctAnswer: Scarcity is reduced for some goods but not eliminated because wants and other constraints remain.
commonError: Assuming productivity growth eliminates scarcity.
feedback: Greater productivity relaxes constraints but does not remove limited resources or competing wants.

q: A store runs out of bottled water after a storm. Which statement is most precise?
options: Scarcity and shortage mean exactly the same thing as the relevant economic conclusion.
The shortage proves scarcity exists only during emergencies as the relevant economic conclusion.
The store has a temporary shortage, while scarcity is the broader condition of limited resources.
The store has no scarcity because water still exists elsewhere for the decision being evaluated.
correctAnswer: The store has a temporary shortage, while scarcity is the broader condition of limited resources.
commonError: Confusing a market shortage with the universal condition of scarcity.
feedback: A shortage is a temporary market imbalance; scarcity is the permanent need to choose among limited resources.

q: During a drought, a city allocates water first to hospitals, then households, and lastly decorative landscaping. The policy most clearly reflects:
options: A market surplus caused by excess supply.
A guarantee that the allocation is both perfectly efficient and perfectly equal.
A scarcity-driven tradeoff among uses with different social priorities.
A claim that water has no opportunity cost.
correctAnswer: A scarcity-driven tradeoff among uses with different social priorities.
commonError: Focusing on one beneficiary while ignoring displaced uses.
feedback: Drought limits the available water, so the city must rank competing uses.

q: A hospital has one intensive-care bed and two equally ill patients. Which conclusion follows from scarcity?
options: Efficiency requires serving both patients fully.
The bed is not scarce because no price is charged.
A fair rule can eliminate the resource constraint.
Any allocation rule will leave at least one valued use unmet.
correctAnswer: Any allocation rule will leave at least one valued use unmet.
commonError: Assuming fairness can remove the underlying constraint.
feedback: Scarcity means not every valued use can be satisfied, regardless of the allocation rule.

q: A policy increases total output but leaves the lowest-income group worse off. Which judgment is most accurate?
options: The policy may improve efficiency while worsening equality.
The policy must improve both efficiency and equality.
The policy eliminates scarcity by increasing output.
The policy cannot be efficient because someone loses.
correctAnswer: The policy may improve efficiency while worsening equality.
commonError: Assuming efficiency and equality are the same criterion.
feedback: Efficiency and distribution are separate dimensions, so they can move in opposite directions.

q: A government reserves scarce vaccine doses for people at highest medical risk rather than for those willing to pay most. The rule primarily changes:
options: How the scarce doses are allocated, not whether the doses are scarce.
The definition of efficiency into equality in the situation described.
The physical supply of doses immediately as the relevant economic conclusion.
The existence of competing wants for vaccination for the decision being evaluated.
correctAnswer: How the scarce doses are allocated, not whether the doses are scarce.
commonError: Believing an allocation rule removes scarcity.
feedback: Allocation rules determine who receives scarce goods; they do not erase the resource limit.

q: An economy can produce more clean energy only by using engineers and materials currently employed elsewhere. Which statement is strongest?
options: Expanding clean energy still requires a tradeoff even if the project has large benefits.
The tradeoff disappears if government finances the project in the situation described.
Large benefits mean no tradeoff exists as the relevant economic conclusion.
Only private firms face scarcity as the relevant economic conclusion.
correctAnswer: Expanding clean energy still requires a tradeoff even if the project has large benefits.
commonError: Assuming socially valuable projects are costless in resource terms.
feedback: Benefits do not eliminate the need to redirect scarce labor and materials from other uses.

q: A reform raises average income and narrows the income gap but requires more administrative resources. Which statement is warranted?
options: Efficiency and equality can never improve together under the stated conditions.
Administrative resources are not scarce because they are publicly funded in the situation described.
The reform may improve both efficiency and equality while still using scarce resources.
The reform has no tradeoff because both outcomes improve for the decision being evaluated.
correctAnswer: The reform may improve both efficiency and equality while still using scarce resources.
commonError: Treating tradeoffs as proof that every objective must worsen.
feedback: Some policies can improve multiple outcomes, but resource use and implementation constraints still matter.

q: A coastal city can use a limited parcel for flood protection, affordable housing, or commercial development. Which analysis best respects scarcity?
options: Compare the benefits and distributional effects of each feasible use while recognizing that choosing one limits the others.
Declare all three uses essential and assume they can be completed fully as the relevant economic conclusion.
Choose the option with the largest visible budget as the relevant economic conclusion.
Treat public ownership as eliminating the tradeoff as the relevant economic conclusion.
correctAnswer: Compare the benefits and distributional effects of each feasible use while recognizing that choosing one limits the others.
commonError: Listing benefits without confronting mutually exclusive uses.
feedback: Scarcity requires comparing feasible alternatives and their efficiency and distributional consequences.

q: A policy expands total production, reduces pollution, and requires a small tax increase. Which statement is most defensible?
options: Multiple benefits mean the policy has no cost as the relevant economic conclusion.
The policy can improve several goals at once, but the tax and resource requirements remain part of the tradeoff.
Scarcity matters only if total production falls as the relevant economic conclusion.
Any tax increase proves the policy is inefficient as the relevant economic conclusion.
correctAnswer: The policy can improve several goals at once, but the tax and resource requirements remain part of the tradeoff.
commonError: Using a single outcome to judge a multi-dimensional policy.
feedback: A complete tradeoff analysis includes gains, resource use, financing, and distribution.

q: Which claim commits the clearest scarcity error?
options: “Higher productivity can relax a resource constraint.” as the relevant economic conclusion.
“A zero money price can still involve time costs.” as the relevant economic conclusion.
“Because digital files can be copied cheaply, producing and distributing them uses no scarce resources.”
“Allocation rules affect who receives scarce goods.” as the relevant economic conclusion.
correctAnswer: “Because digital files can be copied cheaply, producing and distributing them uses no scarce resources.”
commonError: Equating low marginal copying cost with zero resource use.
feedback: Creation, servers, bandwidth, attention, and time remain scarce even when copying is inexpensive.

q: A region faces limited electricity during a heat wave. It can prioritize hospitals, households, or energy-intensive factories. Which response is the most complete economic analysis?
options: Serve whichever group pays the most and call the result automatically fair as the relevant economic conclusion.
Identify the unavoidable allocation tradeoff, compare total benefits, and examine who bears the losses under each rule.
Increase the posted price and ignore physical grid limits as the relevant economic conclusion.
Split electricity equally and conclude scarcity has disappeared as the relevant economic conclusion.
correctAnswer: Identify the unavoidable allocation tradeoff, compare total benefits, and examine who bears the losses under each rule.
commonError: Reducing a scarcity problem to a single efficiency or fairness rule.
feedback: A complete analysis recognizes the physical constraint and evaluates both efficiency and distribution.

q: A government can increase disaster preparedness by diverting engineers from current infrastructure repairs. The preparedness program is highly valuable. What still follows?
options: Public projects do not compete for scarce inputs under the stated conditions.
Its value does not remove the tradeoff created by limited engineering capacity.
Only money, not skilled labor, can be scarce as the relevant economic conclusion.
A valuable program has no resource cost for the decision being evaluated.
correctAnswer: Its value does not remove the tradeoff created by limited engineering capacity.
commonError: Treating high value as proof of no sacrifice.
feedback: Even high-value projects require scarce labor, time, and materials that could serve other purposes.

q: An allocation rule maximizes total output but concentrates nearly all gains among a small group. Which conclusion is strongest?
options: The rule may be efficient by one criterion while raising serious equality concerns.
Scarcity prevents analysts from discussing distribution in the situation described.
The rule is automatically equal because output is high as the relevant economic conclusion.
Any unequal result must reduce total output for the decision being evaluated.
correctAnswer: The rule may be efficient by one criterion while raising serious equality concerns.
commonError: Using efficiency as a complete moral judgment.
feedback: Efficiency and equality are distinct criteria and should be evaluated separately.

q: A breakthrough makes desalination much cheaper, but coastal land, energy, pipelines, and environmental capacity remain limited. Which statement is best?
options: Only consumer wants remain limited after the breakthrough under the stated conditions.
The innovation changes the severity and location of tradeoffs but does not abolish scarcity.
Scarcity ends because one input became cheaper as the relevant economic conclusion.
The innovation converts all scarcity into temporary shortages for the decision being evaluated.
correctAnswer: The innovation changes the severity and location of tradeoffs but does not abolish scarcity.
commonError: Assuming one technological improvement removes all constraints.
feedback: Technology can relax particular constraints while other scarce inputs and competing uses remain.

q: Which statement defines scarcity most accurately?
options: Markets always have shortages.
People never have enough income.
Resources are limited relative to wants.
Every good has a high price.
correctAnswer: Resources are limited relative to wants.
commonError: Confusing scarcity with high prices or low income.
feedback: Scarcity is the condition of limited resources relative to wants.

q: Choosing more of one use for a fixed resource generally means:
options: The market necessarily has a surplus under the stated conditions.
Less of that resource is available for another use.
The resource is no longer scarce as the relevant economic conclusion.
All users become equally well off for the decision being evaluated.
correctAnswer: Less of that resource is available for another use.
commonError: Ignoring displaced uses.
feedback: A fixed resource devoted to one use cannot simultaneously serve another.

q: Efficiency is primarily about:
options: Giving everyone identical outcomes under the stated conditions.
Eliminating every tradeoff in the situation described.
Getting the greatest total value from available resources.
Ensuring no one ever loses from change for the decision being evaluated.
correctAnswer: Getting the greatest total value from available resources.
commonError: Confusing efficiency with equality.
feedback: Efficiency concerns how much total value is produced from scarce resources.

q: A town spends its entire emergency fund on flood barriers instead of fire equipment. The central issue is:
options: An elimination of scarcity through public spending.
A shortage created by a price floor.
A tradeoff among competing uses of limited funds.
A gain from comparative advantage.
correctAnswer: A tradeoff among competing uses of limited funds.
commonError: Ignoring the alternative public use.
feedback: The same limited fund cannot fully finance both priorities.

q: A policy raises total output but widens the income gap. Which pair best describes the possible outcome?
options: Lower efficiency and higher equality.
No change in either criterion.
Scarcity and shortage become identical.
Higher efficiency and lower equality.
correctAnswer: Higher efficiency and lower equality.
commonError: Treating efficiency and equality as one measure.
feedback: Total output and distribution can move in opposite directions.

q: Why does a zero-price service still face scarcity?
options: It uses limited labor, space, equipment, or time.
The service creates no competing uses.
Zero price guarantees unlimited supply.
Only priced goods use resources.
correctAnswer: It uses limited labor, space, equipment, or time.
commonError: Equating free access with unlimited resources.
feedback: Money price and resource scarcity are different issues.

q: A city allocates scarce shelter beds by medical vulnerability instead of willingness to pay. What changes?
options: All tradeoffs disappear.
The number of beds automatically rises.
Efficiency and equality become identical.
The allocation rule changes, while scarcity remains.
correctAnswer: The allocation rule changes, while scarcity remains.
commonError: Assuming rationing rules remove the constraint.
feedback: The rule determines recipients but does not create more beds.

q: A technology raises output and reduces input use, yet firms still choose among projects. Why?
options: Only government choices involve tradeoffs.
Higher output guarantees every project can be funded.
Remaining capital, labor, time, and wants are still limited.
Technology eliminates all scarcity once productivity rises.
correctAnswer: Remaining capital, labor, time, and wants are still limited.
commonError: Assuming productivity growth eliminates choice.
feedback: Productivity relaxes constraints but does not remove all competing uses.

q: Which evaluation is most complete for a policy that increases output but harms a vulnerable group?
options: Reject it solely because one group loses under the stated conditions.
Assume the policy has no tradeoff if output rises in the situation described.
Judge only the change in total output as the relevant economic conclusion.
Assess both the total gains and the distribution of gains and losses.
correctAnswer: Assess both the total gains and the distribution of gains and losses.
commonError: Using only one criterion in a multi-dimensional judgment.
feedback: Economic evaluation should separate efficiency from distributional effects.

q: Scarcity exists when:
options: A seller earns a profit under the stated conditions.
Limited resources cannot satisfy every competing want.
A store temporarily runs out of one item as the relevant economic conclusion.
A price is legally fixed for the decision being evaluated.
correctAnswer: Limited resources cannot satisfy every competing want.
commonError: Confusing scarcity with shortage or regulation.
feedback: Scarcity is the general condition of limited resources relative to wants.

q: Which statement describes efficiency rather than equality?
options: Benefits are distributed equally across groups.
Resources are arranged to produce the greatest total value.
Everyone receives the same share.
Income differences are eliminated.
correctAnswer: Resources are arranged to produce the greatest total value.
commonError: Confusing production efficiency with distributional equality.
feedback: Efficiency focuses on total value from resources.

q: A tradeoff occurs because:
options: Every choice must involve money.
Only governments face constraints.
Using a limited resource one way restricts other uses.
High-benefit choices use no scarce resources.
correctAnswer: Using a limited resource one way restricts other uses.
commonError: Ignoring nonmoney resources and alternative uses.
feedback: Tradeoffs arise whenever scarce resources have competing uses.

q: A library extends weekend hours but must reduce weekday staffing. What does this demonstrate?
options: A market surplus under the stated conditions.
The end of scarcity in the situation described.
A tradeoff in the use of limited staff time.
A guarantee of equal benefits for the decision being evaluated.
correctAnswer: A tradeoff in the use of limited staff time.
commonError: Failing to transfer the tradeoff idea to a service setting.
feedback: More staffing in one period leaves less staffing available in another.

q: A food bank receives more donations but still cannot meet every request. Which conclusion is best?
options: The food bank now faces only a price shortage under the stated conditions.
The additional resources reduce the constraint but do not eliminate scarcity.
No allocation rule is needed after donations rise as the relevant economic conclusion.
Scarcity disappears whenever supply increases for the decision being evaluated.
correctAnswer: The additional resources reduce the constraint but do not eliminate scarcity.
commonError: Assuming more resources remove all unmet wants.
feedback: More resources can ease scarcity while competing needs remain.

q: A student can spend Saturday working for $80 or attending a free concert. If the student attends the concert, the opportunity cost is:
options: The $80 in forgone earnings.
The concert ticket price of $0.
Only the cost of transportation.
Every activity the student could imagine doing.
correctAnswer: The $80 in forgone earnings.
commonError: Looking only for an explicit money payment.
feedback: The next-best alternative is working, so the forgone $80 is the opportunity cost.

q: A city uses an empty lot for a playground instead of a community garden. The opportunity cost of the playground is:
options: The original purchase price of the lot.
The value of the community garden that is not built.
Zero because the city already owns the land.
The total value of every possible project.
correctAnswer: The value of the community garden that is not built.
commonError: Treating owned resources as costless.
feedback: Opportunity cost is the value of the next-best use of the lot.

q: A “free” training session can still have an opportunity cost because participants:
options: Count only past expenses as costs.
Must always pay a hidden fee.
Face no alternatives while attending.
Give up the next-best use of their time.
correctAnswer: Give up the next-best use of their time.
commonError: Equating zero price with zero opportunity cost.
feedback: Time has alternative uses even when no fee is charged.

q: Which alternative determines the opportunity cost of a choice?
options: The least valuable rejected alternative.
All alternatives added together.
The most valuable alternative that is given up.
Only alternatives with a money price.
correctAnswer: The most valuable alternative that is given up.
commonError: Adding every forgone option instead of selecting the next best.
feedback: Opportunity cost is based on the single next-best forgone alternative.

q: A worker can take a one-day class, work an overtime shift earning $180, or attend a recreational event valued at $120. If the worker takes the class, the opportunity cost is:
options: $300, the sum of both rejected alternatives.
$180, the value of the next-best alternative.
$120, because recreation is not work.
Zero if the class has no tuition.
correctAnswer: $180, the value of the next-best alternative.
commonError: Adding all forgone alternatives.
feedback: The overtime shift is the most valuable forgone option, so it determines opportunity cost.

q: An entrepreneur leaves a job paying $55,000 to run a business that earns $70,000 after paying all explicit expenses. Ignoring nonmoney benefits, the economic profit is:
commonError: Ignoring forgone salary as an implicit cost.
feedback: Economic profit subtracts the $55,000 forgone salary from the $70,000 accounting profit.

q: A student pays $12,000 in tuition and gives up $24,000 in earnings to attend school for a year. The opportunity cost is at least:
commonError: Counting only tuition or only forgone earnings.
feedback: The full opportunity cost includes explicit tuition and forgone earnings.

q: A farmer can plant wheat worth $42,000 or soybeans worth $50,000 on the same field. If wheat is planted, the opportunity cost is:
options: $42,000 under the stated conditions.
$92,000 in the situation described.
$8,000 as the relevant economic conclusion.
$50,000 in forgone soybean output.
correctAnswer: $50,000 in forgone soybean output.
commonError: Using the difference rather than the value of the next-best alternative.
feedback: The next-best alternative is the soybean crop worth $50,000.

q: A firm uses a warehouse it owns for storage instead of renting it out for $30,000 per year. The storage decision has an implicit cost of:
options: The original construction cost only.
$0 because the firm owns the warehouse.
The value of all buildings in the area.
$30,000 per year.
correctAnswer: $30,000 per year.
commonError: Treating owned resources as free.
feedback: Forgone rental income is an implicit opportunity cost.

q: A consultant can accept Project A for a net benefit of $18,000, Project B for $15,000, or Project C for $9,000. If Project A is chosen, its opportunity cost is:
commonError: Summing all rejected alternatives or using the chosen benefit.
feedback: Project B is the highest-valued forgone alternative.

q: A restaurant owner uses a building she owns. Comparable rent is $40,000, and she gives up a $60,000 salaried job. The business earns $120,000 after explicit expenses. Economic profit is:
commonError: Ignoring one or both implicit costs.
feedback: Economic profit is $120,000 minus $40,000 forgone rent minus $60,000 forgone salary.

q: A student values a research assistantship at $6,000, a summer job at $7,500, and travel at $5,000. Choosing the assistantship has an opportunity cost of:
commonError: Adding all alternatives or choosing the least valuable.
feedback: The summer job is the next-best forgone alternative.

q: A government uses $20 million of idle-looking land for a courthouse. The land could be sold for $14 million or used for housing valued at $18 million. The opportunity cost is:
options: $32 million.
$20 million.
$14 million.
$18 million.
correctAnswer: $18 million.
commonError: Using the purchase budget or adding rejected uses.
feedback: The housing project is the most valuable forgone use.

q: A worker’s hourly wage rises from $20 to $32. Holding preferences constant, the opportunity cost of taking an unpaid hour off:
options: Stays at zero because no payment is made.
Rises by the value of every other activity combined.
Rises from $20 to $32.
Falls because leisure is now more valuable.
correctAnswer: Rises from $20 to $32.
commonError: Failing to update opportunity cost when the next-best alternative changes.
feedback: The forgone wage from an hour of work is now larger.

q: A nonprofit receives a donated building and chooses to use it as offices rather than lease it for $90,000 annually. Which statement is correct?
options: The opportunity cost is the donor’s original purchase price under the stated conditions.
The opportunity cost is zero because the building was donated in the situation described.
The donation has no purchase price, but office use carries a $90,000 annual opportunity cost.
The opportunity cost includes every possible future use added together for the decision being evaluated.
correctAnswer: The donation has no purchase price, but office use carries a $90,000 annual opportunity cost.
commonError: Equating acquisition price with current opportunity cost.
feedback: Current opportunity cost is based on the best forgone use, here the lease income.

q: A physician can spend an evening treating patients for $1,200, teaching a seminar valued at $900, or attending a family event valued at $1,100. If she teaches the seminar, the opportunity cost is:
commonError: Adding alternatives or using the chosen activity’s value.
feedback: Treating patients is the highest-valued forgone alternative.

q: A firm owns a machine that can produce Product X with contribution margin $75,000 or Product Y with contribution margin $92,000. Converting it to Product Z yields $100,000 but costs $15,000. If the firm chooses Z, what is the net benefit relative to the next-best alternative?
commonError: Comparing gross returns without subtracting conversion cost and the next-best alternative.
feedback: Z nets $85,000, which is $7,000 below the $92,000 next-best use.

q: A graduate program charges $28,000 tuition. A student would otherwise earn $46,000 and values lost leisure at $6,000. Ignoring future benefits, the one-year opportunity cost is:
commonError: Omitting forgone earnings or nonmoney value.
feedback: The full cost is tuition plus forgone earnings plus the value of lost leisure.

q: A firm can use a patent internally for expected profit of $3.2 million, license it for $3.8 million, or sell it for $3.5 million. Internal use requires an additional $0.4 million development cost. Relative to the next-best alternative, internal use has a net advantage of:
options: $3.4 million.
-$1.0 million.
-$0.2 million.
$0.6 million.
correctAnswer: -$1.0 million.
commonError: Ignoring the development cost or comparing with the wrong alternative.
feedback: Internal use nets $2.8 million; licensing at $3.8 million is the next-best alternative.

q: A public agency assigns a skilled team to a bridge project worth $14 million instead of a flood project worth $16 million or a transit project worth $11 million. The bridge project’s opportunity cost is:
options: $14 million.
$16 million.
$27 million.
$2 million.
correctAnswer: $16 million.
commonError: Using the difference or summing all forgone alternatives.
feedback: The flood project is the highest-valued forgone alternative.

q: A self-employed designer earns $95,000 after explicit expenses but gives up a $72,000 salary and could rent the home studio for $18,000. Economic profit is:
commonError: Ignoring forgone salary or rental income.
feedback: Economic profit is $95,000 minus $72,000 minus $18,000.

q: A worker rejects jobs paying $140 and $110 to attend a workshop. The workshop’s opportunity cost is:
options: $0 if the workshop is free.
commonError: Adding all rejected options or ignoring forgone wages.
feedback: The highest-valued forgone alternative determines opportunity cost.

q: A firm uses owned office space that could rent for $24,000. What implicit cost belongs in the decision?
options: The value of every available office.
$24,000 in forgone rent.
$0 because the space is owned.
The building’s original purchase price.
correctAnswer: $24,000 in forgone rent.
commonError: Treating owned resources as costless.
feedback: Forgone rent is the opportunity cost of using the space.

q: Tuition is $10,000 and forgone earnings are $30,000. The minimum opportunity cost of attending school is:
commonError: Counting only explicit or implicit cost.
feedback: Both tuition and forgone earnings are part of the full cost.

q: A firm chooses a project yielding $48,000 over alternatives yielding $52,000 and $41,000. Its opportunity cost is:
commonError: Using the difference or summing alternatives.
feedback: The best forgone project yields $52,000.

q: A business earns $160,000 after explicit expenses. The owner gives up a $90,000 salary and $35,000 in rent. Economic profit is:
commonError: Ignoring implicit costs.
feedback: Subtract both forgone salary and rent from accounting profit.

q: An owned parcel can support a clinic worth $12 million, housing worth $15 million, or parking worth $5 million. Choosing the clinic has an opportunity cost of:
options: $12 million.
$3 million.
$20 million.
$15 million.
correctAnswer: $15 million.
commonError: Adding alternatives or using the chosen project’s value.
feedback: Housing is the highest-valued forgone use.

q: Opportunity cost is the value of:
options: Every rejected alternative added together.
The next-best alternative given up.
A past cost that cannot be recovered.
Only the money price of the choice.
correctAnswer: The next-best alternative given up.
commonError: Using total forgone options or explicit price only.
feedback: Opportunity cost is the value of the single next-best forgone alternative.

q: A free event can have an opportunity cost because:
options: Only paid activities have alternatives under the stated conditions.
Attending uses time that could have been used elsewhere.
Past spending determines the cost as the relevant economic conclusion.
Free events use no scarce resources for the decision being evaluated.
correctAnswer: Attending uses time that could have been used elsewhere.
commonError: Equating zero price with zero opportunity cost.
feedback: Time and other resources have alternative uses even when admission is free.

q: An owner uses a building that could rent for $2,000 per month. The implicit cost is:
options: The original purchase price each month.
All possible rents added together.
$2,000 per month.
$0 because the owner owns it.
correctAnswer: $2,000 per month.
commonError: Ignoring forgone rental income.
feedback: The best forgone rental income is an implicit opportunity cost.

q: A volunteer shift replaces a paid shift worth $90. What is the opportunity cost of volunteering?
options: Zero because volunteering is unpaid.
Only transportation expenses.
$90 in forgone earnings.
$180 because both activities matter.
correctAnswer: $90 in forgone earnings.
commonError: Failing to transfer the idea to unpaid activity.
feedback: The paid shift is the next-best forgone alternative.

q: A school uses a field for parking instead of athletics. The field’s opportunity cost is:
options: The value of the best athletic use forgone.
The cost of every possible use added together.
Only the cost of paving.
Zero because the school owns the field.
correctAnswer: The value of the best athletic use forgone.
commonError: Treating owned land as costless.
feedback: The next-best forgone use determines opportunity cost.

q: A decision should be expanded by one more unit when:
options: A large amount has already been spent under the stated conditions.
Total benefit is positive in the situation described.
Marginal benefit is at least as large as marginal cost.
Average benefit exceeds average cost for the decision being evaluated.
correctAnswer: Marginal benefit is at least as large as marginal cost.
commonError: Using averages, totals, or sunk costs instead of marginal values.
feedback: The marginal rule compares the added benefit with the added cost of the next unit.

q: A student has already paid a nonrefundable fee for a course. When deciding whether to continue, the fee should be treated as:
options: The opportunity cost of the next class meeting under the stated conditions.
A marginal benefit of continuing in the situation described.
A sunk cost that does not change the current marginal decision.
A reason to continue no matter what for the decision being evaluated.
correctAnswer: A sunk cost that does not change the current marginal decision.
commonError: Letting an unrecoverable past cost control a current choice.
feedback: Only future benefits and future costs should guide the current decision.

q: Marginal benefit means:
options: A cost that has already been paid.
The additional benefit from one more unit.
The average benefit per unit.
The total benefit from all units.
correctAnswer: The additional benefit from one more unit.
commonError: Confusing marginal with total or average.
feedback: Marginal benefit is the change in total benefit from one additional unit.

q: A café should remain open for one extra hour if the extra revenue from that hour:
options: Exceeds average revenue for the day.
Covers yesterday’s losses.
Exceeds total daily cost.
Exceeds the extra operating cost for that hour.
correctAnswer: Exceeds the extra operating cost for that hour.
commonError: Comparing the next-hour benefit with total or past costs.
feedback: The extra hour should be judged by its additional revenue and additional cost.

q: The marginal benefit of the fourth unit is $18 and its marginal cost is $14. The fourth unit should be:
options: Produced or consumed because marginal benefit exceeds marginal cost.
Rejected because total cost is positive in the situation described.
Accepted only if no sunk cost exists as the relevant economic conclusion.
Rejected unless average benefit also rises for the decision being evaluated.
correctAnswer: Produced or consumed because marginal benefit exceeds marginal cost.
commonError: Using total or average values instead of the next unit.
feedback: The fourth unit adds $4 in net benefit.

q: A firm has already spent $50,000 developing a product. Finishing it will cost another $12,000 and is expected to generate $18,000. The firm should:
options: Cancel because total spending would reach $62,000 under the stated conditions.
Finish only to avoid wasting the $50,000 in the situation described.
Finish the product because the future benefit exceeds the future cost.
Ignore the expected revenue because it is uncertain for the decision being evaluated.
correctAnswer: Finish the product because the future benefit exceeds the future cost.
commonError: Including sunk development spending in the marginal comparison.
feedback: The $50,000 is unrecoverable; the relevant comparison is $18,000 versus $12,000.

q: A museum stays open an extra hour. The added admissions revenue is $900 and added staffing and utility cost is $1,100. Marginal analysis says:
options: Stay open because total daily revenue is high under the stated conditions.
Stay open to recover fixed building costs in the situation described.
Close at the normal time because marginal cost exceeds marginal benefit.
Close only if average cost rises for the decision being evaluated.
correctAnswer: Close at the normal time because marginal cost exceeds marginal benefit.
commonError: Using totals or fixed costs rather than incremental values.
feedback: The extra hour reduces net benefit by $200.

q: Which statement best distinguishes marginal cost from average cost?
options: Average cost measures only fixed cost as the relevant economic conclusion.
Marginal cost is the cost of one more unit; average cost is total cost per unit.
The two measures are identical at every output as the relevant economic conclusion.
Marginal cost is always lower than average cost for the decision being evaluated.
correctAnswer: Marginal cost is the cost of one more unit; average cost is total cost per unit.
commonError: Treating marginal and average values as interchangeable.
feedback: Marginal and average costs answer different questions.

q: A student studies an additional hour. The expected grade benefit is valued at 9 points and fatigue cost at 6 points. The net marginal benefit is:
options: 3 points.
15 points.
6 points.
9 points.
correctAnswer: 3 points.
commonError: Adding benefit and cost or reporting only one side.
feedback: Net marginal benefit equals 9 minus 6.

q: A firm can produce units with marginal benefits of $20, $16, $12, and $8 and marginal costs of $6, $10, $13, and $15. How many units maximize net benefit?
options: Two units.
Four units.
One unit.
Three units.
correctAnswer: Two units.
commonError: Continuing after marginal cost exceeds marginal benefit.
feedback: The first two units add net benefit; the third and fourth would reduce it.

q: A city has spent $4 million on a stadium design. Construction will cost another $30 million and generate benefits valued at $24 million. What should marginal analysis recommend?
options: Build because total benefits are positive.
Do not build because the future cost exceeds the future benefit.
Ignore construction cost because design work is complete.
Build because abandoning the design wastes $4 million.
correctAnswer: Do not build because the future cost exceeds the future benefit.
commonError: Using sunk design cost to justify a negative future decision.
feedback: The $4 million is sunk; the relevant comparison is $24 million in benefits versus $30 million in future cost.

q: A clinic can extend hours. The first extra hour has MB $5,000 and MC $2,000; the second has MB $3,000 and MC $2,500; the third has MB $1,500 and MC $2,200. The optimal extension is:
options: Zero hours.
Three hours.
One hour.
Two hours.
correctAnswer: Two hours.
commonError: Using total benefit without checking each additional hour.
feedback: Extend through the second hour and stop before the third, where MC exceeds MB.

q: A company’s average profit per customer is positive, but the next customer is expected to cost $140 to serve and generate $110 in revenue. The company should:
options: Accept to spread fixed costs as the relevant economic conclusion.
Accept because average profit is positive in the situation described.
Accept because total revenue will rise as the relevant economic conclusion.
Reject the next customer because marginal cost exceeds marginal benefit.
correctAnswer: Reject the next customer because marginal cost exceeds marginal benefit.
commonError: Using average profitability to justify a negative marginal transaction.
feedback: The next customer lowers profit by $30.

q: A farmer has already applied fertilizer. One additional unit raises crop value by $45 and costs $38, but also causes $10 in expected runoff damage. Including the external cost, the farmer should:
options: Ignore runoff because it is not paid directly by the farmer.
Apply because total crop value is positive.
Apply because private marginal cost is only $38.
Not apply the additional unit because marginal social cost is $48.
correctAnswer: Not apply the additional unit because marginal social cost is $48.
commonError: Ignoring a relevant marginal cost borne by others.
feedback: The added social cost is $38 plus $10, which exceeds the $45 marginal benefit.

q: A software team has spent six months on a feature. Completing it requires 200 more hours and is expected to save users 140 hours. The strongest decision is:
options: Stop unless there are additional future benefits not yet counted.
Continue because six months have already been invested.
Ignore the remaining 200 hours because the project is nearly done.
Continue because users receive some benefit.
correctAnswer: Stop unless there are additional future benefits not yet counted.
commonError: Escalating commitment based on past effort.
feedback: Past effort is sunk; the remaining cost exceeds the identified future benefit.

q: A factory’s next three pollution-control units have marginal benefits of $90, $70, and $45 and marginal costs of $40, $65, and $60. How many units should be installed?
options: One unit.
Three units.
Zero units.
Two units.
correctAnswer: Two units.
commonError: Installing every beneficial unit without comparing the final unit’s marginal cost.
feedback: The first two units have MB at least as large as MC; the third does not.

q: A project already cost $8 million. Finishing costs $5 million. Expected future benefits are $4 million, but cancellation requires a $0.5 million cleanup cost. What is the best choice?
options: Cancel, because cancellation costs $0.5 million while finishing has a $1 million negative future net benefit.
Finish because future benefits exceed cleanup cost as the relevant economic conclusion.
Cancel because total project cost exceeds total benefit as the relevant economic conclusion.
Finish to avoid wasting the $8 million as the relevant economic conclusion.
correctAnswer: Cancel, because cancellation costs $0.5 million while finishing has a $1 million negative future net benefit.
commonError: Ignoring the relevant alternatives after a sunk cost.
feedback: Compare future choices: finish yields -$1 million; cancel costs $0.5 million.

q: A university can admit one more student. Tuition revenue is $18,000, added instructional and support cost is $15,000, and expected congestion cost to other students is $4,000. The marginal social decision is:
options: Do not admit because marginal social cost is $19,000.
Admit because total enrollment revenue is positive.
Admit because congestion is not a direct budget expense.
Admit because tuition exceeds the university’s private cost.
correctAnswer: Do not admit because marginal social cost is $19,000.
commonError: Ignoring external marginal cost.
feedback: The added social cost exceeds the marginal benefit by $1,000.

q: A transit agency can add buses. Marginal rider benefits for buses 1–5 are $120k, $100k, $80k, $55k, and $35k; marginal costs are $60k, $70k, $75k, $65k, and $50k. How many buses maximize net benefit?
options: Three buses.
Four buses.
Two buses.
Five buses.
correctAnswer: Three buses.
commonError: Stopping based on total benefit or continuing after the next unit has negative net benefit.
feedback: The first three buses have MB at least as high as MC; the fourth does not.

q: A firm spent $12 million on a prototype. Completing it costs $7 million. Selling the finished product yields $6 million, while selling the unfinished prototype now yields $1.5 million. What should the firm do?
options: Abandon both options because total spending is already too high as the relevant economic conclusion.
Finish to recover the $12 million as the relevant economic conclusion.
Sell the unfinished prototype because finishing produces $1 million less than the current alternative.
Finish because $6 million exceeds $1.5 million as the relevant economic conclusion.
correctAnswer: Sell the unfinished prototype because finishing produces $1 million less than the current alternative.
commonError: Comparing gross future revenue without considering the alternative and remaining cost.
feedback: Finishing nets -$1 million relative to now, while selling the prototype yields $1.5 million.

q: A hospital considers one more diagnostic test. Expected patient benefit is $420, direct test cost is $250, and expected false-positive follow-up cost is $190. The marginal social decision is:
options: Ignore false-positive costs because they occur later.
Do not add the test because total marginal cost is $440.
Add because the direct cost is below the benefit.
Add because some patients benefit.
correctAnswer: Do not add the test because total marginal cost is $440.
commonError: Ignoring expected downstream marginal cost.
feedback: Relevant marginal cost includes direct and expected follow-up costs.

q: A producer has positive total profit at 100 units. Unit 101 adds $72 in revenue and $88 in cost. What should the producer do?
options: Stop at 100 units.
Produce unit 101 to lower average fixed cost.
Produce unit 101 because total profit is positive.
Produce until total revenue begins to fall.
correctAnswer: Stop at 100 units.
commonError: Using total profit or average cost rather than the marginal comparison.
feedback: Unit 101 reduces profit because its marginal cost exceeds its marginal revenue.

q: A policy has already spent $2 billion. Continuing for one year costs $600 million and produces expected benefits of $520 million; ending it costs $30 million in transition expenses. What is the best marginal choice?
options: End the policy because $30 million is less costly than an $80 million negative continuation margin.
End because total cost exceeds total benefit since inception as the relevant economic conclusion.
Continue to avoid wasting the $2 billion as the relevant economic conclusion.
Continue because benefits exceed transition costs as the relevant economic conclusion.
correctAnswer: End the policy because $30 million is less costly than an $80 million negative continuation margin.
commonError: Letting sunk spending or an irrelevant total comparison drive the decision.
feedback: The decision should compare future alternatives: continue loses $80 million; ending costs $30 million.

q: The next unit has marginal benefit $24 and marginal cost $19. What should happen?
options: Continue only because past costs are sunk.
Stop because cost is positive.
Stop unless average benefit rises.
Produce or consume the next unit.
correctAnswer: Produce or consume the next unit.
commonError: Rejecting a unit whenever it has any cost.
feedback: The next unit adds $5 in net benefit.

q: A nonrefundable fee has already been paid. It should affect the current decision:
options: Only if some part of it can still be recovered or avoided.
Only when total benefits are positive.
Always, because past spending must be recovered.
Never, even if a refund remains available.
correctAnswer: Only if some part of it can still be recovered or avoided.
commonError: Using a blanket rule without checking whether the cost is truly sunk.
feedback: A cost is sunk only when it cannot be recovered or changed.

q: Marginal analysis compares:
options: Average benefit and average cost only.
Total benefit and total cost only.
The added benefit and added cost of the next unit.
Past benefit and past cost.
correctAnswer: The added benefit and added cost of the next unit.
commonError: Confusing marginal with total or average analysis.
feedback: The marginal question is what changes if one more unit is chosen.

q: MB values are 30, 22, 14, 8 and MC values are 10, 16, 15, 12. What quantity is optimal?
options: One unit.
Four units.
Three units.
Two units.
correctAnswer: Two units.
commonError: Continuing past the point where MC exceeds MB.
feedback: The first two units add net benefit; the third does not.

q: A project’s past cost is $5 million. Finishing costs $3 million and creates $2 million in future benefits. The correct decision is:
options: Finish to recover the past cost.
Finish because total benefits are positive.
Do not finish.
Ignore the remaining cost because work has begun.
correctAnswer: Do not finish.
commonError: Escalating commitment based on sunk cost.
feedback: The future marginal cost exceeds the future marginal benefit.

q: The next customer generates $150 in revenue, $120 in direct cost, and $40 in congestion cost for others. The social decision is:
options: Reject the customer.
Accept because congestion is not paid by the firm.
Accept because revenue exceeds direct cost.
Accept because private profit is $30.
correctAnswer: Reject the customer.
commonError: Ignoring external marginal cost.
feedback: Marginal social cost is $160, which exceeds the $150 benefit.

q: Marginal benefit is:
options: The added benefit from one more unit.
A past benefit that cannot change.
Average benefit per unit.
Total benefit from all units.
correctAnswer: The added benefit from one more unit.
commonError: Confusing marginal, total, and average values.
feedback: Marginal benefit measures the change from one additional unit.

q: A cost is sunk when it:
options: Will occur only if one more unit is chosen.
Has already occurred and cannot be recovered.
Changes with the current decision.
Equals the next-best alternative.
correctAnswer: Has already occurred and cannot be recovered.
commonError: Calling future or avoidable costs sunk.
feedback: Sunk costs are past and unrecoverable.

q: The marginal rule says to continue while:
options: Marginal benefit is at least as large as marginal cost.
Average cost is falling in the situation described.
Total benefit is positive as the relevant economic conclusion.
Past spending is large for the decision being evaluated.
correctAnswer: Marginal benefit is at least as large as marginal cost.
commonError: Using totals, averages, or sunk costs.
feedback: The next unit should be chosen when its added benefit covers its added cost.

q: An extra tutoring session is expected to improve performance by 7 points and creates 4 points of fatigue cost. What is the net marginal benefit?
options: 3 points.
4 points.
11 points.
7 points.
correctAnswer: 3 points.
commonError: Failing to subtract marginal cost from marginal benefit.
feedback: Net marginal benefit is 7 minus 4.

q: A company has spent heavily on a failing product. Future revenue is $40,000 and future completion cost is $55,000. What should it do?
options: Continue because much has already been spent.
Stop development unless another future benefit exists.
Continue because revenue is positive.
Ignore future cost because the project is nearly complete.
correctAnswer: Stop development unless another future benefit exists.
commonError: Failing to transfer sunk-cost reasoning to a business case.
feedback: Past spending is irrelevant; the future cost exceeds the future benefit.

q: In the CPI, the base-year index is usually set equal to:
options: The current inflation rate.
commonError: Forgetting the index convention for the base year.
feedback: The base-year basket cost is indexed to 100.

q: If the CPI is 125, the fixed consumer basket costs:
options: 25 dollars more in every economy.
75 percent less than in the base year.
25 percent more than in the base year.
125 percent more than in the base year.
correctAnswer: 25 percent more than in the base year.
commonError: Reading the index level as a percentage increase of the same size.
feedback: A CPI of 125 means the basket cost is 1.25 times its base-year cost.

q: The inflation rate from one year to the next uses:
options: The percentage change in real GDP.
The percentage change in the CPI.
The dollar change in the CPI basket only.
The CPI level divided by 100 with no comparison.
correctAnswer: The percentage change in the CPI.
commonError: Using an index-point change instead of a percentage change.
feedback: Inflation is the percentage change in the CPI across periods.

q: A fixed market basket costs $240 in the base year and $240 this year. The CPI is:
commonError: Treating no price change as a zero index.

q: A basket costs $500 in the base year and $575 today. Today’s CPI is:
commonError: Using the dollar increase rather than the basket-cost ratio.

q: The CPI rises from 150 to 159. The inflation rate is:
options: 5.7 percent.
159 percent.
6 percent.
9 percent.
correctAnswer: 6 percent.
commonError: Using the 9-point index change as the inflation rate.
feedback: Inflation = (159 − 150)/150 = 6 percent.

q: A basket cost $360 in the base year. If the CPI is 140, the current basket cost is:
commonError: Multiplying or dividing the index incorrectly.
feedback: Current cost = 1.40 × $360 = $504.

q: The CPI falls from 200 to 190. The inflation rate is:
options: 95 percent.
-10 percent.
-5 percent.
5 percent.
correctAnswer: -5 percent.
commonError: Using the point change or ignoring the sign.
feedback: The percentage change is (190 − 200)/200 = -5 percent.

q: A fixed basket contains twice as many units of food as transportation. Food prices rise 10 percent and transportation prices do not change. Which statement is best?
options: The CPI must rise exactly 10 percent as the relevant economic conclusion.
Transportation receives the larger weight because its price did not change in the situation described.
The CPI cannot change unless every item price changes as the relevant economic conclusion.
The basket cost rises, with food receiving greater weight because more units are in the basket.
correctAnswer: The basket cost rises, with food receiving greater weight because more units are in the basket.
commonError: Ignoring basket quantities when combining price changes.
feedback: CPI weights reflect the quantities in the fixed basket, so the larger food quantity matters more.

q: Index audit: the base-year basket cost is $640, last year’s CPI was 125, and the basket costs $856 now. Which pair gives the current CPI and inflation since last year?
options: 133.75 and 8.75 percent.
856 and 33.75 percent.
133.75 and 7 percent.
125 and 7 percent.
correctAnswer: 133.75 and 7 percent.
commonError: Using the base-year cost in the inflation denominator.
feedback: Current CPI is 100 × 856/640 = 133.75; inflation is (133.75 − 125)/125 = 7 percent.

q: The CPI is 132 and the current basket costs $924. What was the base-year basket cost?
commonError: Multiplying by the index instead of dividing by 1.32.

q: A basket contains 4 units of A and 6 units of B. Base prices are $5 and $10; current prices are $8 and $12. What is the CPI?
commonError: Averaging price changes without using basket quantities.
feedback: Base cost is $80; current cost is $104; CPI = 130.

q: The CPI rises from 180 to 189 and then to 198.45. Which statement is correct?
options: Inflation is 5 percent in each period.
Inflation accelerates from 5 to 9.45 percent.
Inflation is 9 percent and then 9.45 percent.
Inflation is 10.25 percent in both periods.
correctAnswer: Inflation is 5 percent in each period.
commonError: Comparing index-point changes rather than percentage changes.
feedback: Each increase is 5 percent of the previous CPI level.

q: A base-year basket costs $1,000. Current prices make it cost $1,275. If next year the same basket costs $1,326, next year’s inflation rate is:
options: 4 percent.
27.5 percent.
32.6 percent.
5.1 percent.
correctAnswer: 4 percent.
commonError: Using the base-year basket cost rather than the current-year cost as the denominator.
feedback: The CPI moves from 127.5 to 132.6, a 4 percent increase.

q: A basket has 10 units of food and 1 unit of electronics. Food prices rise 4 percent and the electronics price rises 40 percent. Which conclusion is justified without more information?
options: Food must dominate because there are more units as the relevant economic conclusion.
The CPI change depends on the dollar expenditure weights, not just the percentage changes.
The CPI must rise 40 percent as the relevant economic conclusion.
The two percentage changes should be averaged equally for the decision being evaluated.
correctAnswer: The CPI change depends on the dollar expenditure weights, not just the percentage changes.
commonError: Using quantities or percentage changes alone without dollar weights.
feedback: The contribution of each item depends on quantity times price in the basket.

q: The CPI is reported as 130 and the base-year basket cost is $400. What is the current basket cost?
commonError: Using the dollar difference or inverting the ratio.
feedback: Current cost = 1.30 × $400 = $520.

q: The CPI moves from 125 to 135. The inflation rate is:
options: 10 percent.
135 percent.
7.4 percent.
8 percent.
correctAnswer: 8 percent.
commonError: Using the 10-point change as the percentage rate.
feedback: Inflation = 10/125 = 8 percent.

q: If the CPI is 160, a base-year basket costing $300 now costs:
commonError: Treating the index as a dollar amount.
feedback: Current cost = 1.60 × $300 = $480.

q: The CPI moves from 120 to 127.2. What inflation rate does that imply?
options: 5.7 percent.
7.2 percent.
127.2 percent.
6 percent.
correctAnswer: 6 percent.
commonError: Using the base-year cost or point change as the denominator.
feedback: Inflation = (127.2 − 120)/120 = 6 percent.

q: A basket has 3 units of X and 2 units of Y. Base prices are $10 and $20; current prices are $14 and $25. The CPI is:
commonError: Averaging price changes instead of calculating basket costs.
feedback: Base cost is $70 and current cost is $92, so CPI is about 131.4.

q: The CPI is 144 and the current basket costs $1,080. The base-year cost is:
commonError: Multiplying by 1.44 rather than dividing.

q: A price-index report lists last year’s CPI as 120. The base-year basket cost is $900 and the same basket costs $1,188 this year. Which pair gives this year’s CPI and inflation rate?
options: 132 and 12 percent.
118.8 and 10 percent.
120 and 10 percent.
132 and 10 percent.
correctAnswer: 132 and 10 percent.
commonError: Using index points or the base year as the inflation denominator.
feedback: This year’s CPI is 100 × 1,188/900 = 132; inflation is (132 − 120)/120 = 10 percent.

q: A fixed basket has 5 units of A and 4 units of B. Base prices are $8 and $15. Current prices are $10 and $18. Next year prices are $11 and $19. What are the current CPI and next year’s inflation rate?
options: 122 and 10 percent.
122 and 32 percent.
122 and about 8.2 percent.
132 and about 8.2 percent.
correctAnswer: 122 and about 8.2 percent.
commonError: Failing to calculate both basket costs before finding the percentage change.
feedback: Base cost is $100, current cost $122, and next cost $132; inflation is 10/122, about 8.2 percent.

q: For a commercial bank, customer deposits are recorded as:
options: Revenue because deposits increase cash.
Liabilities because the bank owes the funds to depositors.
Bank capital because deposits belong to shareholders.
Assets because the bank physically holds the money.
correctAnswer: Liabilities because the bank owes the funds to depositors.
commonError: Treating deposits as bank-owned assets.
feedback: Deposits are liabilities: the bank has an obligation to repay depositors.

q: A 10 percent reserve rule applies to a $50,000 deposit base. How much must the bank keep rather than lend?
commonError: Multiplying by the lending share instead of the reserve ratio.
feedback: Ten percent of $50,000 is $5,000.

q: When a bank makes a loan from excess reserves, the loan is recorded as:
options: Bank capital only.
An asset of the bank.
A reduction in deposits with no matching asset.
A liability of the bank.
correctAnswer: An asset of the bank.
commonError: Classifying loans as liabilities.
feedback: Borrowers owe repayment to the bank, so loans are bank assets.

q: If the reserve requirement rises, the simple money multiplier generally:
options: Rises.
Stays equal to one.
Falls.
Becomes unrelated to reserves.
correctAnswer: Falls.
commonError: Reversing the relationship between the reserve ratio and multiplier.
feedback: The simple multiplier is 1 divided by the reserve ratio.

q: A bank has $300,000 in deposits, a 12 percent reserve requirement, and $50,000 in actual reserves. Excess reserves are:
commonError: Forgetting to subtract required reserves from actual reserves.
feedback: Required reserves are $36,000, leaving $14,000 in excess reserves.

q: A new $2,000 deposit enters a bank with a 20 percent reserve requirement. The bank’s maximum first-round loan is:
commonError: Using required reserves as lending or applying the multiplier to the first round.
feedback: The bank keeps $400 and may lend $1,600.

q: The simple money multiplier is 5. The implied reserve ratio is:
options: 50 percent.
25 percent.
20 percent.
5 percent.
correctAnswer: 20 percent.
commonError: Using the multiplier itself as the reserve percentage.
feedback: The reserve ratio is 1/5, or 20 percent.

q: A bank receives a new deposit and holds all of it as excess reserves instead of lending. Compared with the simple multiplier prediction:
options: Deposit expansion will be larger.
The reserve requirement becomes zero.
Deposit expansion will be smaller.
Deposit expansion must equal the full multiplier.
correctAnswer: Deposit expansion will be smaller.
commonError: Assuming banks always lend all excess reserves.
feedback: The simple multiplier is a maximum that depends on lending and redepositing.

q: A bank reports $14 million in assets and $12.9 million in liabilities. What is its capital cushion?
options: $26.9 million.
$1.1 million.
$14 million.
$12.9 million.
correctAnswer: $1.1 million.
commonError: Adding assets and liabilities or using liabilities alone.
feedback: Bank capital equals assets minus liabilities: $1.1 million.

q: A borrower spends a newly created bank loan, and the recipient deposits the payment at another bank. This process:
options: Eliminates the original loan under the stated conditions.
Creates a new deposit that can support another round of lending.
Prevents any further money creation as the relevant economic conclusion.
Turns the loan into bank capital for the decision being evaluated.
correctAnswer: Creates a new deposit that can support another round of lending.
commonError: Failing to connect lending, spending, and redepositing.
feedback: Loan proceeds commonly become deposits elsewhere, allowing additional lending.

q: A bank has $800,000 in deposits, a 10 percent reserve requirement, and $95,000 in reserves. If deposits increase by $100,000 and reserves rise by $20,000, the bank’s new excess reserves are:
commonError: Updating deposits or reserves but not both.
feedback: New deposits are $900,000, required reserves are $90,000, and actual reserves are $115,000.

q: A bank has $25 million in assets and $1.5 million in capital. An 8 percent asset loss occurs. What is the new capital position?
options: $0.5 million.
-$0.5 million.
-$2.0 million.
$1.5 million.
correctAnswer: -$0.5 million.
commonError: Applying the loss to capital instead of assets.
feedback: An 8 percent asset loss is $2 million, reducing $1.5 million of capital to -$0.5 million.

q: A banking system has a 10 percent reserve requirement, but banks hold an additional 5 percent of deposits as excess reserves and the public holds no currency. A simple effective deposit multiplier is closest to:
commonError: Ignoring voluntary excess reserves.
feedback: If 15 percent of deposits is retained, the simple effective multiplier is about 1/0.15 = 6.67.

q: Deposits are $600,000, the reserve requirement is 10 percent, and actual reserves are $90,000. Excess reserves are:
commonError: Failing to subtract required reserves.
feedback: Required reserves are $60,000, leaving $30,000.

q: A simple money multiplier of 4 corresponds to what reserve ratio?
options: 25 percent.
4 percent.
20 percent.
40 percent.
correctAnswer: 25 percent.
commonError: Using the percentage rather than its reciprocal.
feedback: The reserve ratio is the reciprocal of the multiplier: 1/4 = 25 percent.

q: A bank makes a loan from excess reserves. On the bank’s balance sheet, the new loan is:
options: A withdrawal.
Capital.
An asset.
A liability.
correctAnswer: An asset.
commonError: Misclassifying a bank loan.
feedback: The borrower owes the bank, so the loan is an asset.

q: A bank has $1.5 million in deposits, a 12 percent reserve requirement, and $240,000 in reserves. Its maximum immediate new lending is:
options: $1.32 million.
commonError: Confusing required reserves with excess reserves.
feedback: Required reserves are $180,000, so excess reserves are $60,000.

q: A bank has $30 million in assets and $28.5 million in liabilities. Assets fall 6 percent. New capital is:
options: $1.5 million.
-$1.8 million.
-$0.3 million.
$0.3 million.
correctAnswer: -$0.3 million.
commonError: Applying the asset loss to the wrong base.
feedback: Initial capital is $1.5 million; the asset loss is $1.8 million.

q: A $10,000 deposit enters a system with a 20 percent reserve requirement. If banks lend all excess reserves and loans are redeposited, maximum total deposits are:
commonError: Confusing first-round lending with total deposit expansion.
feedback: The multiplier is 5, so total deposits can rise by $50,000.

q: Congress increases government purchases by $80 billion while households cut consumption by $50 billion for unrelated reasons. Before multiplier effects, the net direct change in aggregate demand is:
options: A $30 billion decrease.
No change.
A $30 billion increase.
A $130 billion increase.
correctAnswer: A $30 billion increase.
commonError: Adding changes without respecting their directions.
feedback: Government purchases add $80 billion while consumption subtracts $50 billion.

q: A $120 billion tax rebate is issued and households spend 65 percent of the added disposable income initially. What is the first-round consumption increase?
options: $42 billion.
$184.6 billion.
$78 billion.
$120 billion.
correctAnswer: $78 billion.
commonError: Using the MPS or the full tax cut as first-round consumption.
feedback: First-round consumption is 0.65 × $120 billion = $78 billion.

q: A government raises taxes and increases purchases by the same dollar amount. Which statement is most precise about the immediate AD effects?
options: The two actions must cancel exactly before behavior is considered.
Both actions shift AD right by the same amount.
Taxes enter AD directly as a negative component.
Purchases enter AD directly, while higher taxes reduce consumption indirectly.
correctAnswer: Purchases enter AD directly, while higher taxes reduce consumption indirectly.
commonError: Treating taxes as a direct component of aggregate demand.
feedback: Government purchases are part of AD; taxes work through disposable income and consumption.

q: A temporary tax cut is mostly saved because households expect it to be reversed next year. Compared with a tax cut that is mostly spent, the AD shift is:
options: Smaller.
Necessarily leftward.
Identical.
Larger.
correctAnswer: Smaller.
commonError: Ignoring household spending behavior.
feedback: A smaller consumption response weakens the tax cut’s effect on aggregate demand.

q: The government cuts purchases during a recession but also cuts taxes. Which conclusion is valid without knowing the magnitudes and household response?
options: Aggregate demand must rise.
The two policies always cancel exactly.
The net direction of aggregate demand is ambiguous.
Aggregate demand must fall.
correctAnswer: The net direction of aggregate demand is ambiguous.
commonError: Assuming one policy label determines the combined outcome.
feedback: A spending cut shifts AD left, while a tax cut tends to shift it right; magnitudes matter.

q: A tax increase of $60 billion reduces consumption by $42 billion in the first round. The implied MPC is:
commonError: Dividing in the wrong direction or using the MPS.
feedback: MPC = $42 billion / $60 billion = 0.70.

q: A fiscal package raises government purchases by $120 billion and taxes by $100 billion. If MPC = 0.8, the package’s first-round effect on AD is:
options: A $20 billion increase.
A $200 billion increase.
A $40 billion increase.
A $40 billion decrease.
correctAnswer: A $40 billion increase.
commonError: Ignoring that the tax increase reduces consumption by MPC times the tax change.
feedback: Purchases add $120 billion; the tax increase reduces consumption by $80 billion.

q: A tax cut is announced, but credit-constrained households spend 90 percent while high-income households spend 30 percent. Which feature matters most for the AD effect?
options: The long-run natural rate of output as the relevant economic conclusion.
Whether government purchases are counted in GDP as the relevant economic conclusion.
Only the statutory size of the tax cut as the relevant economic conclusion.
How the tax cut is distributed across groups with different marginal propensities to consume.
correctAnswer: How the tax cut is distributed across groups with different marginal propensities to consume.
commonError: Assuming every dollar of tax reduction produces the same consumption response.
feedback: The aggregate consumption response depends on who receives the tax cut and how much they spend.

q: A government increases purchases by $50 billion and raises taxes by $50 billion. MPC is 0.75. Before subsequent multiplier rounds, the net first-round AD change is:
options: No change.
A $12.5 billion increase.
A $37.5 billion decrease.
A $100 billion increase.
correctAnswer: A $12.5 billion increase.
commonError: Assuming equal spending and tax changes have equal direct AD effects.
feedback: Purchases add $50 billion; the tax increase cuts consumption by $37.5 billion.

q: A tax cut raises disposable income by $160 billion. Households spend 60 percent of the increase initially. If later rounds follow a simple spending multiplier of 2.5, the total AD increase before other offsets is:
options: $400 billion.
$64 billion.
$240 billion.
$96 billion.
correctAnswer: $240 billion.
commonError: Applying the multiplier to the full tax cut instead of the first-round consumption change.
feedback: First-round consumption rises $96 billion; multiplying by 2.5 gives $240 billion.

q: The government increases infrastructure purchases, but imports rise sharply because much of the equipment is purchased abroad. Relative to a package using domestic inputs, the increase in domestic aggregate demand is likely:
options: Leftward because any import increase reduces government purchases.
Identical because all government spending counts equally.
Smaller because part of the spending leaks into imports.
Larger because imports are part of domestic production.
correctAnswer: Smaller because part of the spending leaks into imports.
commonError: Ignoring import leakage from domestic demand.
feedback: Spending on imports does not directly purchase domestically produced output.

q: A tax cut and transfer increase have the same budget cost. The transfer is targeted to households with a higher MPC. Which package is likely to shift AD more in the short run?
options: The targeted transfer increase.
Neither can affect consumption.
They must have identical effects.
The broad tax cut regardless of spending behavior.
correctAnswer: The targeted transfer increase.
commonError: Ignoring differences in marginal propensity to consume.
feedback: More of the targeted transfer is likely to be spent, producing a larger initial consumption increase.

q: A government plans contractionary fiscal policy. Which combination most clearly supports that goal?
options: Lower taxes and unchanged purchases.
Higher transfers and lower taxes.
Higher government purchases and lower taxes.
Lower government purchases and higher taxes.
correctAnswer: Lower government purchases and higher taxes.
commonError: Mixing expansionary and contractionary tools.
feedback: Lower purchases and higher taxes both push aggregate demand left.

q: A recessionary economy receives a temporary tax rebate. Households use half to repay debt, save one quarter, and spend one quarter. The immediate consumption channel equals:
options: 50 percent of the rebate.
100 percent of the rebate.
75 percent of the rebate.
25 percent of the rebate.
correctAnswer: 25 percent of the rebate.
commonError: Treating saving or debt repayment as immediate consumption.
feedback: Only the portion spent on current consumption directly raises the consumption component of AD.

q: Expansionary fiscal policy most directly includes:
options: Higher government purchases or lower taxes.
Lower government purchases or higher taxes.
Higher reserve requirements only.
Lower consumer confidence.
correctAnswer: Higher government purchases or lower taxes.
commonError: Confusing fiscal policy with monetary policy or private behavior.
feedback: Expansionary fiscal policy raises government demand or supports private spending.

q: Which fiscal action shifts aggregate demand left through lower disposable income?
options: A tax cut.
A tax increase.
Higher government purchases.
Higher transfer payments.
correctAnswer: A tax increase.
commonError: Reversing the effect of taxes on disposable income and consumption.
feedback: A tax increase reduces disposable income and tends to reduce consumption.

q: Government purchases are:
options: The same as household saving.
A direct component of aggregate demand.
A direct component of short-run aggregate supply.
Excluded from GDP.
correctAnswer: A direct component of aggregate demand.
commonError: Misplacing government purchases in the macro model.
feedback: Government purchases are included directly in C + I + G + NX.

q: A $100 billion tax cut with MPC 0.8 raises first-round consumption by:
options: $500 billion.
$80 billion.
$20 billion.
$100 billion.
correctAnswer: $80 billion.
commonError: Using the MPS or multiplier too early.
feedback: MPC times the tax cut gives the first-round consumption increase.

q: A cut in government purchases shifts AD left because it directly reduces:
options: Labor-force participation under the stated conditions.
The money multiplier in the situation described.
The government-purchases component of spending.
The economy’s productive capacity for the decision being evaluated.
correctAnswer: The government-purchases component of spending.
commonError: Confusing an AD shift with an AS or banking change.
feedback: Government purchases enter aggregate demand directly.

q: A tax cut has a weak AD effect when households:
options: Spend most of it immediately.
Save most of the increase in disposable income.
Face a high marginal propensity to consume.
Increase consumption by more than the tax cut.
correctAnswer: Save most of the increase in disposable income.
commonError: Ignoring the consumption response.
feedback: More saving means less immediate consumption and a smaller rightward AD shift.

q: Government purchases rise $90 billion and taxes rise $60 billion. MPC is 0.75. What is the net first-round change in AD?
options: A $135 billion increase.
A $45 billion increase.
A $30 billion increase.
A $45 billion decrease.
correctAnswer: A $45 billion increase.
commonError: Failing to distinguish the direct spending effect from the tax-induced consumption effect.
feedback: Purchases add $90 billion; taxes reduce consumption by $45 billion.

q: A $200 billion tax cut reaches two equal groups. One group spends 80 percent and the other spends 40 percent. What is the combined first-round consumption increase?
options: $160 billion.
$120 billion.
$240 billion.
$80 billion.
correctAnswer: $120 billion.
commonError: Applying one group’s MPC to the entire tax cut.
feedback: Each group receives $100 billion; spending rises $80 billion plus $40 billion.

q: A decrease in household wealth, holding other factors constant, shifts aggregate demand:
options: Not at all because wealth is not part of spending.
Up along the same AD curve.
Left.
Right.
correctAnswer: Left.
commonError: Confusing a spending shifter with a movement along AD.
feedback: Lower wealth tends to reduce consumption, shifting aggregate demand left.

q: A lower domestic price level makes domestic goods relatively cheaper to foreign buyers. This supports the downward slope of AD through the:
options: Sticky-wage effect.
Productivity effect.
Exchange-rate effect.
Wealth effect.
correctAnswer: Exchange-rate effect.
commonError: Confusing the three reasons aggregate demand slopes downward.
feedback: A lower domestic price level can lower interest rates and the currency value, raising net exports.

q: Consumer confidence rises while firms become more pessimistic about future sales. What can be concluded about aggregate demand?
options: The net direction is ambiguous without knowing the sizes of the consumption and investment changes.
Aggregate demand must shift left as the relevant economic conclusion.
The economy moves down along the same AD curve as the relevant economic conclusion.
Aggregate demand must shift right as the relevant economic conclusion.
correctAnswer: The net direction is ambiguous without knowing the sizes of the consumption and investment changes.
commonError: Letting one shifter determine the combined result.
feedback: Confidence raises consumption, while pessimism lowers investment; magnitudes determine the net shift.

q: The price level falls, but taxes rise at the same time. Which statement is most precise?
options: Both changes cause movement along AD.
The price-level change shifts AD right and the tax increase shifts AD left.
The price-level change causes movement along AD, while the tax increase shifts AD left.
Both changes shift AD left.
correctAnswer: The price-level change causes movement along AD, while the tax increase shifts AD left.
commonError: Confusing a change in the price level with a nonprice AD shifter.
feedback: The price level is on the graph’s vertical axis; taxes are an external shifter.

q: Foreign income falls sharply while domestic firms increase investment. The effect on domestic aggregate demand is:
options: A certain rightward shift under the stated conditions.
A certain leftward shift in the situation described.
Ambiguous because net exports fall while investment rises.
A movement upward along AD for the decision being evaluated.
correctAnswer: Ambiguous because net exports fall while investment rises.
commonError: Ignoring offsetting components of aggregate demand.
