feedback: Lower foreign income reduces exports, while higher investment raises AD.

q: A higher price level increases money demand, which raises interest rates and reduces investment. This sequence explains:
options: A rightward shift of LRAS under the stated conditions.
A rightward shift of AD in the situation described.
A leftward shift of SRAS as the relevant economic conclusion.
A movement upward and leftward along the existing AD curve.
correctAnswer: A movement upward and leftward along the existing AD curve.
commonError: Treating the interest-rate effect as a shift of AD.
feedback: The interest-rate effect is one reason quantity of real GDP demanded falls as the price level rises.

q: A depreciation of the domestic currency occurs for reasons unrelated to the domestic price level. Holding other factors constant, aggregate demand shifts:
options: Left because net exports fall.
Left because domestic goods become more expensive to foreigners.
Right because exports rise and imports fall.
Nowhere because exchange rates matter only along AD.
correctAnswer: Right because exports rise and imports fall.
commonError: Reversing the net-export effect of currency depreciation.
feedback: A weaker domestic currency tends to raise net exports and aggregate demand.

q: A rise in the price level reduces the real value of household money balances. The immediate AD implication is:
options: Higher net exports and a rightward AD shift.
Higher consumption and a rightward AD shift.
Lower consumption and a movement upward along AD.
Lower investment and a leftward SRAS shift.
correctAnswer: Lower consumption and a movement upward along AD.
commonError: Confusing the wealth effect with an AD shifter.
feedback: The wealth effect reduces quantity of output demanded as the price level rises.

q: A country experiences higher consumer confidence, lower expected business profits, and a rise in foreign income. Which components of AD move first?
options: All four components rise automatically.
Only government purchases change.
Consumption falls, investment rises, and net exports fall.
Consumption and net exports rise, while investment falls.
correctAnswer: Consumption and net exports rise, while investment falls.
commonError: Failing to trace each shifter to the correct AD component.
feedback: Confidence affects consumption, expected profits affect investment, and foreign income affects exports.

q: The price level rises at the same time that the government cuts taxes. Which graph description is correct?
options: Only movement along AD occurs as the relevant economic conclusion.
There is movement downward along AD plus a leftward shift in the situation described.
Only a rightward shift occurs as the relevant economic conclusion.
There is movement upward along AD plus a rightward shift of the AD curve.
correctAnswer: There is movement upward along AD plus a rightward shift of the AD curve.
commonError: Treating simultaneous movement and shift as mutually exclusive.
feedback: The price-level change causes movement along AD; the tax cut shifts the curve.

q: Domestic interest rates fall because the central bank expands money supply, while foreign income also falls. What can be said about AD?
options: Investment tends to rise and net exports tend to fall, so the net shift is ambiguous.
Only a movement along AD occurs as the relevant economic conclusion.
AD must shift left as the relevant economic conclusion.
AD must shift right as the relevant economic conclusion.
correctAnswer: Investment tends to rise and net exports tend to fall, so the net shift is ambiguous.
commonError: Ignoring offsetting investment and net-export effects.
feedback: The two shifters push different AD components in opposite directions.

q: A student says, “Any fall in real GDP means AD shifted left.” What is the best correction?
options: The statement is always correct as the relevant economic conclusion.
Real GDP can fall from movement along AD or from shifts in AD or AS; the graph cause must be identified.
Real GDP changes only when AD shifts as the relevant economic conclusion.
A fall in real GDP always means SRAS shifted right as the relevant economic conclusion.
correctAnswer: Real GDP can fall from movement along AD or from shifts in AD or AS; the graph cause must be identified.
commonError: Inferring a curve shift from an outcome without identifying the cause.
feedback: Observed output changes do not by themselves reveal which curve moved.

q: The domestic price level rises, consumer confidence strengthens, and foreign income declines. Which analysis is complete?
options: AD shifts left with no offsetting force as the relevant economic conclusion.
There is movement upward along AD, a rightward pressure from consumption, and a leftward pressure from net exports.
AD shifts right with no movement along it as the relevant economic conclusion.
All changes move the economy along the same AD curve as the relevant economic conclusion.
correctAnswer: There is movement upward along AD, a rightward pressure from consumption, and a leftward pressure from net exports.
commonError: Collapsing simultaneous movement and multiple shifts into one effect.
feedback: The price level changes quantity demanded; confidence and foreign income shift the curve in opposite directions.

q: A lower price level raises the real value of money balances, lowers interest rates, and makes domestic goods cheaper relative to foreign goods. What happens along AD?
options: Consumption, investment, and net exports all tend to rise.
All three channels shift AD rather than cause movement along it.
Consumption falls while investment and net exports rise.
Only government purchases rise.
correctAnswer: Consumption, investment, and net exports all tend to rise.
commonError: Misclassifying the three slope mechanisms.
feedback: The wealth, interest-rate, and exchange-rate effects all raise quantity of real GDP demanded at a lower price level.

q: Businesses become optimistic, households become pessimistic, and the currency depreciates. Which AD components are initially affected?
options: Only consumption changes.
Investment rises, consumption falls, and net exports rise.
Government purchases and LRAS change.
Investment falls, consumption rises, and net exports fall.
correctAnswer: Investment rises, consumption falls, and net exports rise.
commonError: Assigning shifters to the wrong spending components.
feedback: Expectations affect I and C, while depreciation affects NX.

q: A tax increase and higher government purchases occur together. Which statement is justified without numerical information?
options: The two policies push aggregate demand in opposite directions.
AD must shift left as the relevant economic conclusion.
The policies cause only movement along AD as the relevant economic conclusion.
AD must shift right as the relevant economic conclusion.
correctAnswer: The two policies push aggregate demand in opposite directions.
commonError: Assuming a combined policy has a predetermined net effect.
feedback: Higher G raises AD; higher taxes tend to reduce consumption and AD.

q: The price level is unchanged, but desired consumption, investment, and net exports all decline. The economy experiences:
options: Movement upward along AD.
A rightward shift of short-run aggregate supply.
Movement downward along AD.
A leftward shift of aggregate demand.
correctAnswer: A leftward shift of aggregate demand.
commonError: Using movement-along language when the price level is held fixed.
feedback: At a given price level, lower planned spending shifts AD left.

q: A country’s currency appreciates and foreign economies enter recession while domestic consumer confidence rises. The net AD effect is:
options: Certainly leftward as the relevant economic conclusion.
Certainly rightward as the relevant economic conclusion.
Ambiguous because consumption rises while net exports fall for two reasons.
No change because the effects cancel exactly for the decision being evaluated.
correctAnswer: Ambiguous because consumption rises while net exports fall for two reasons.
commonError: Assuming offsetting forces are equal without evidence.
feedback: Confidence raises C, while appreciation and lower foreign income reduce NX.

q: Households become more confident about future income and increase planned consumption at every price level. What happens?
options: Short-run aggregate supply shifts right.
Aggregate demand shifts left.
There is movement up along aggregate demand.
Aggregate demand shifts right.
correctAnswer: Aggregate demand shifts right.
commonError: Confusing movement along AD with a rightward shift.
feedback: Higher planned consumption at each price level shifts aggregate demand right.

q: The horizontal axis of an AD-AS graph measures:
options: The nominal interest rate.
Real output.
The price level.
The money supply.
correctAnswer: Real output.
commonError: Reversing the graph axes.
feedback: Real GDP or real output appears on the horizontal axis.

q: A higher price level, by itself, causes:
options: A leftward shift of AD.
A rightward shift of AD.
A rightward shift of LRAS.
Movement upward along the AD curve.
correctAnswer: Movement upward along the AD curve.
commonError: Treating the price level as an AD shifter.
feedback: The price level is on the vertical axis, so its change causes movement along AD.

q: Firms expect stronger future sales. Aggregate demand shifts:
options: Left through lower investment.
Nowhere because expectations affect only SRAS.
Right through higher investment.
Right through lower net exports.
correctAnswer: Right through higher investment.
commonError: Linking business expectations to the wrong component.
feedback: More optimistic firms tend to increase investment spending.

q: A higher price level reduces real money balances and consumption. This is the:
options: Sticky-wage effect.
Wealth effect.
Multiplier effect.
Exchange-rate effect.
correctAnswer: Wealth effect.
commonError: Confusing the slope mechanisms.
feedback: The wealth effect works through the purchasing power of money holdings.

q: Foreign income falls. Domestic aggregate demand tends to:
options: Move down along AD.
Shift right because imports fall.
Shift left because exports fall.
Stay fixed because foreign income is not domestic.
correctAnswer: Shift left because exports fall.
commonError: Ignoring export demand from foreign buyers.
feedback: Lower foreign income reduces demand for domestic exports.

q: The price level falls while firms cut investment. What occurs?
options: Only movement upward along AD under the stated conditions.
Only a rightward AD shift in the situation described.
Movement downward along AD plus a leftward AD shift.
A rightward SRAS shift only for the decision being evaluated.
correctAnswer: Movement downward along AD plus a leftward AD shift.
commonError: Failing to separate price-level movement from a spending shift.
feedback: The lower price level changes quantity demanded; lower investment shifts AD left.

q: Consumer confidence rises and the currency appreciates. The net AD direction is:
options: No change because the effects are equal under the stated conditions.
Ambiguous because consumption rises while net exports fall.
Certainly rightward as the relevant economic conclusion.
Certainly leftward for the decision being evaluated.
correctAnswer: Ambiguous because consumption rises while net exports fall.
commonError: Assuming offsetting shifters cancel exactly.
feedback: The two components move in opposite directions, and magnitudes matter.

q: Why does a higher price level reduce investment along AD?
options: Higher prices reduce expected input costs.
Higher prices automatically lower taxes.
Higher money demand tends to raise interest rates.
Higher prices directly raise productive capacity.
correctAnswer: Higher money demand tends to raise interest rates.
commonError: Confusing AD slope with supply-side changes.
feedback: The interest-rate effect links a higher price level to less investment.

q: The price level rises, taxes fall, and foreign income falls. Which description is correct?
options: A single rightward shift as the relevant economic conclusion.
Only movement along AD as the relevant economic conclusion.
Movement upward along AD, a rightward tax-cut shift, and a leftward net-export shift.
A single leftward shift as the relevant economic conclusion.
correctAnswer: Movement upward along AD, a rightward tax-cut shift, and a leftward net-export shift.
commonError: Combining three distinct forces into one curve change.
feedback: The price level causes movement; taxes and foreign income shift AD in opposite directions.

q: Consumer confidence falls, investment expectations improve, and the currency depreciates. Which components move?
options: Only government purchases rise.
All components fall.
Consumption falls, investment rises, and net exports rise.
Consumption rises, investment falls, and net exports fall.
correctAnswer: Consumption falls, investment rises, and net exports rise.
commonError: Mapping shifters to the wrong components.
feedback: Confidence affects C, business expectations affect I, and depreciation affects NX.

q: A lower price level raises real balances, lowers interest rates, and weakens the currency. Which AD result follows?
options: SRAS shifts right because interest rates fell under the stated conditions.
Consumption, investment, and net exports tend to rise along the curve.
Only consumption rises as the relevant economic conclusion.
AD shifts right because the price level fell for the decision being evaluated.
correctAnswer: Consumption, investment, and net exports tend to rise along the curve.
commonError: Treating movement along AD as a curve shift.
feedback: All three classic channels raise quantity demanded at the lower price level.

q: A rise in economy-wide productivity shifts long-run aggregate supply:
options: Not at all because productivity affects only demand.
Left.
Right.
Up along the same curve.
correctAnswer: Right.
commonError: Confusing productive capacity with aggregate demand.
feedback: Higher productivity raises the economy’s sustainable level of output.

q: An increase in nominal wages, holding productivity and expected prices constant, shifts short-run aggregate supply:
options: Nowhere.
Down along the same SRAS curve.
Right.
Left.
correctAnswer: Left.
commonError: Reversing the effect of higher production costs.
feedback: Higher nominal wages raise firms’ costs and reduce output supplied at each price level.

q: If workers and firms expect a higher price level before contracts are set, short-run aggregate supply tends to:
options: Become vertical immediately.
Remain fixed because expectations affect only AD.
Shift left.
Shift right.
correctAnswer: Shift left.
commonError: Reversing the expected-price effect.
feedback: Higher expected prices tend to produce higher nominal wages and other input costs.

q: A temporary payroll-tax reduction lowers firms’ labor costs. Holding other factors constant, SRAS shifts:
options: AD right only.
LRAS left only.
Left.
Right.
correctAnswer: Right.
commonError: Treating a production-cost change as an AD shifter.
feedback: Lower per-worker cost raises short-run output supplied at each price level.

q: Why can an unexpected rise in the price level increase output in the short run under sticky-wage theory?
options: Household wealth rises and shifts AD as the relevant economic conclusion.
Potential output permanently increases as the relevant economic conclusion.
Nominal wages immediately rise more than prices as the relevant economic conclusion.
Product prices rise before nominal wages fully adjust, lowering real labor cost.
correctAnswer: Product prices rise before nominal wages fully adjust, lowering real labor cost.
commonError: Confusing short-run wage rigidity with long-run capacity.
feedback: With sticky wages, unexpected price increases can make production temporarily more profitable.

q: A hurricane destroys factories and transport infrastructure. Which long-run effect is most likely?
options: LRAS shifts left because productive capacity falls.
SRAS shifts right because inputs are scarcer.
LRAS shifts right because rebuilding spending rises.
Only AD shifts right.
correctAnswer: LRAS shifts left because productive capacity falls.
commonError: Focusing on reconstruction spending while ignoring lost capacity.
feedback: Destroyed capital reduces the economy’s potential output.

q: Oil prices rise sharply, but firms also adopt a productivity-enhancing technology. What can be concluded about SRAS?
options: SRAS must shift left as the relevant economic conclusion.
The net shift is ambiguous because costs rise while productivity improves.
Only LRAS can change as the relevant economic conclusion.
SRAS must shift right as the relevant economic conclusion.
correctAnswer: The net shift is ambiguous because costs rise while productivity improves.
commonError: Allowing one supply shifter to dominate without magnitude information.
feedback: Higher oil costs push SRAS left, while higher productivity pushes it right.

q: Expected prices rise by 4 percent, but nominal wages are locked in long-term contracts. Compared with a setting where wages adjust immediately, the leftward SRAS shift is likely:
options: Larger.
Smaller in the short run.
A rightward shift of LRAS.
Identical by definition.
correctAnswer: Smaller in the short run.
commonError: Ignoring the mechanism through which expectations affect costs.
feedback: If wages cannot yet adjust, expected-price changes have a weaker immediate cost effect.

q: A permanent increase in the labor force raises potential output, while a temporary surge in energy prices raises costs. Which combination is most likely?
options: LRAS shifts right and SRAS shifts left.
LRAS shifts left and SRAS shifts right.
Both curves shift left.
Both curves shift right.
correctAnswer: LRAS shifts right and SRAS shifts left.
commonError: Combining long-run capacity and short-run cost changes incorrectly.
feedback: More labor raises capacity; higher energy prices reduce short-run supply.

q: The price level rises unexpectedly while nominal wages are fixed. In the short run, firms tend to:
options: Increase production because output prices rise relative to wage costs.
Leave output unchanged because SRAS is vertical in the situation described.
Shift LRAS right immediately as the relevant economic conclusion.
Reduce production because real wages rise for the decision being evaluated.
correctAnswer: Increase production because output prices rise relative to wage costs.
commonError: Reversing the real-wage effect.
feedback: Unexpectedly higher output prices lower the real cost of contracted wages.

q: A government permanently improves transportation infrastructure but finances it with a temporary business-energy surcharge. Which supply effects are possible?
options: Only AD can change.
LRAS may shift right while SRAS shifts left temporarily.
Both LRAS and SRAS must shift left permanently.
LRAS must remain fixed because taxes are involved.
correctAnswer: LRAS may shift right while SRAS shifts left temporarily.
commonError: Treating all policy effects as demand-side or same-direction.
feedback: Infrastructure can raise capacity while the temporary surcharge raises current production costs.

q: Firms revise expected prices downward after a period of unexpectedly low inflation. Holding actual prices fixed, SRAS tends to:
options: Become vertical.
Shift left.
Shift right.
Move upward along the same curve.
correctAnswer: Shift right.
commonError: Reversing how lower expected prices affect wage and cost setting.
feedback: Lower expected prices tend to reduce nominal wage and input-cost growth.

q: A country receives a permanent productivity improvement and a temporary spike in imported input prices. Which graph change best fits?
options: Both curves shift left permanently under the stated conditions.
LRAS shifts left and SRAS right in the situation described.
Only aggregate demand shifts as the relevant economic conclusion.
LRAS shifts right, while SRAS may shift left initially.
correctAnswer: LRAS shifts right, while SRAS may shift left initially.
commonError: Failing to separate permanent capacity from temporary production costs.
feedback: Productivity raises potential output; costly imported inputs can reduce short-run supply.

q: Workers expect 6 percent inflation, but actual inflation is 2 percent and wage contracts reflect the higher expectation. What happens to SRAS relative to contracts based on accurate expectations?
options: SRAS is farther left because nominal labor costs are higher than necessary.
AD shifts right as the relevant economic conclusion.
SRAS is farther right because real wages are lower as the relevant economic conclusion.
LRAS shifts left as the relevant economic conclusion.
correctAnswer: SRAS is farther left because nominal labor costs are higher than necessary.
commonError: Ignoring how excessive expected inflation enters wage contracts.
feedback: Higher expected prices can produce higher nominal wages and lower short-run supply.

q: A severe storm destroys capital, while emergency deregulation lowers current compliance costs. Which conclusion is strongest?
options: LRAS shifts left, while the SRAS effect is ambiguous because cost relief offsets disruption.
LRAS shifts right because regulation falls as the relevant economic conclusion.
Only AD changes as the relevant economic conclusion.
Both curves must shift left by the same amount as the relevant economic conclusion.
correctAnswer: LRAS shifts left, while the SRAS effect is ambiguous because cost relief offsets disruption.
commonError: Assuming all supply forces have the same horizon and direction.
feedback: Capital destruction lowers capacity; lower compliance cost pushes SRAS right, while storm disruption may push it left.

q: A student says, “Any rise in the price level shifts SRAS right.” What is the best correction?
options: Any price-level rise shifts aggregate demand left only as the relevant economic conclusion.
A change in the actual price level causes movement along SRAS; expected prices or costs shift the curve.
Actual prices shift LRAS, not SRAS as the relevant economic conclusion.
The statement is correct in every case as the relevant economic conclusion.
correctAnswer: A change in the actual price level causes movement along SRAS; expected prices or costs shift the curve.
commonError: Confusing movement along SRAS with a curve shift.
feedback: The actual price level is an axis variable, not a supply shifter by itself.

q: A permanent tax credit raises capital investment, while a temporary wage subsidy lowers current labor costs. Which supply changes are most likely?
options: LRAS shifts right over time and SRAS shifts right immediately.
SRAS shifts left because subsidies raise wages in the situation described.
LRAS shifts left and SRAS right as the relevant economic conclusion.
Only AD shifts right for the decision being evaluated.
correctAnswer: LRAS shifts right over time and SRAS shifts right immediately.
commonError: Failing to distinguish capacity growth from current cost reduction.
feedback: More capital raises potential output, while the subsidy lowers short-run production cost.

q: Expected inflation rises, productivity improves, and oil prices fall. What can be concluded about SRAS?
options: Only LRAS changes as the relevant economic conclusion.
SRAS must shift left as the relevant economic conclusion.
SRAS must shift right as the relevant economic conclusion.
The direction is ambiguous because expectations push left while productivity and cheaper oil push right.
correctAnswer: The direction is ambiguous because expectations push left while productivity and cheaper oil push right.
commonError: Ignoring offsetting supply shifters.
feedback: Multiple cost and productivity forces push SRAS in opposite directions.

q: A country loses 5 percent of its capital stock but gains a technology that raises remaining capital productivity by 8 percent. What is the LRAS implication?
options: The net LRAS effect is ambiguous without knowing the relative output effects.
LRAS must shift right because productivity rose more in percentage terms.
LRAS cannot change when two forces offset.
LRAS must shift left because capital fell.
correctAnswer: The net LRAS effect is ambiguous without knowing the relative output effects.
commonError: Comparing raw percentages that apply to different economic quantities.

q: Nominal wages are fixed for one year. The price level rises unexpectedly, then wage contracts reset to reflect the higher expected price level. What sequence is most likely?
options: A rightward SRAS shift followed by movement down under the stated conditions.
Only aggregate demand changes as the relevant economic conclusion.
An immediate rightward LRAS shift as the relevant economic conclusion.

feedback: Unexpected prices initially raise output along SRAS; higher wage expectations later shift SRAS left.

q: A permanent improvement in education raises worker productivity, but a new regulation raises current compliance costs. Which statement is most complete?
